head: 44bc26cdbdfde0e4543f70ed21db5c6ddea4c1ce
source:
readcost raised a TypeError in `_markdown` on any inline footnote, `^[text]`. markdown-it's footnote plugin builds the footnote's paragraph at the end of the token stream with no line map. A regex such as `^[a-z]` in a doc comment or a Markdown file parses as one. This dropped three files from the draw for the kinds precision test (#103): a Python docstring, a TypeScript doc comment and a Markdown file.

Fix: before reading, a token without a map gets one. The footnote's paragraph takes the line of its `^[` in the paragraph that holds it; any other token without a map takes the map of the nearest enclosing token that has one. The words after an inline footnote also had wrong offsets, because the reference was skipped by searching for `[^`; that is fixed, and the offsets fuzz test now includes inline footnotes.

Guard: an extraction error on one file becomes a note on that file's result, and any other error on one file is reported for that file. The other files are still checked. The exit status stays 2, as `test_crash_exits_2_not_the_findings_code` requires, so a file that was not checked does not pass.

Tested: the three dropped files (same blobs as the draw records) crash on main and check cleanly on this branch. The regression tests use made-up fixtures with the same shapes, and all of them fail on main. The full suite passes locally.

Not changed: GitHub does not render `^[...]` as a footnote, so in a README a regex like `^[a-z]` loses those characters from its sentence. Turning inline footnotes off (`footnote_plugin(inline=False)`) would change what readcost reads, so it is left for a measured change.

head: 67e47abe4901b3f86036338166b42cd449b9ca04
source:
Two extraction bugs and one mismatch between code and docs.

- Notebooks. `readcost check nb.ipynb` read the raw JSON as text, keys and all. A new `notebook` format reads the Markdown cells. With `comments = "all"` it also reads comments in code cells, using the kernel's language (`kernelspec.language`, else `language_info.name`). Outputs and raw cells are skipped. A small JSON reader built on the standard library keeps the offset of every string, so offsets, lines and columns point at the characters inside the `.ipynb` file. An escaped character maps to its whole escape. Bad JSON gives a note and no findings. The default `include` globs still leave notebooks out.
- Languages. A suffix missing from `LANG_BY_EXT` fell through to `text`, so code was read as prose. This adds comment syntax for PHP, Lua, Haskell, Elixir, Julia, R, Dart, Zig and Perl (POD), each with the way it writes doc comments. It also adds a few extensions to the existing C and `#` families. Swift, Kotlin, Scala and shell were already there, and they keep their old rules. A list of other code extensions (`.lisp`, `.sql`, `.css`, ...) now gives a note and no findings. A file with no extension is read by its `#!` line. Prose in `.txt` files, or in files with no extension, is still read as text.
- Inline comments. docs/research.md said findings in comments that `comments = "all"` reads are at info. The code kept each rule's own level (a stacked-nouns warn in a Python `#` comment, as the report found). I changed the code to match the docs, not the reverse. The research doc gives reasons for treating these comments as weaker, and the setting is opt-in, so default output does not change. A level set in config or a flag still wins. C-family and shell comments are read by default, so they keep their levels. The same table said `@param` lines are skipped in doc comments; they are not (checked on a Java fixture), so I corrected the docs there.
- Also fixed: the `#!` line of a shell script was read as a comment.

Tests: `tests/test_formats.py`, made-up fixtures for each language, and notebook tests that check line and column in concise, LSP and SARIF output.

Not sure about:
- The comment readers use regular expressions, not a parser. Comment markers inside strings and nested block comments can be misread; docs/configuration.md lists the known cases.
- The list of code extensions is a judgment call (`.d`, `.v` and `.m` each have more than one meaning).
- No measurement supports the info level for inline comments. It follows the doc's reasons, not labelled data.

head: 6af92432f1651c0fab6d0772523c022dfe887e4a
source:
docs/evaluation.md ("Agents editing in a loop") found that agents fed readcost's feedback either fix the findings in one round or get stuck: they leave a finding they judge wrong while the hook repeats it, or they alternate between two wordings around it. The hooks re-checked and re-reported after every edit, and in block mode PreToolUse could deny the same finding again and again.

What changes (default `hooks.repeat = "once"`; `"always"` keeps the old behaviour):

- Claude Code PostToolUse reports only findings not yet reported for that file in this session, with one line counting the older ones it left out. If every finding is old, it says nothing.
- In block mode a finding blocks or denies once. A repeat gets one advisory line instead. PreToolUse lets the same edit through on the next attempt, and the deny reason tells the model so. piku's PreToolUse follows the same rules.
- A finding is its rule plus its flagged words, lowercased without punctuation, so it survives moving or rewording the text around it.
- The key is `session_id`, else `transcript_path`, plus `agent_id` for a subagent. Without a session there is no memory and every report repeats, so findings are never hidden from a session the hook cannot identify.
- State: one JSON file of hashes per session under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/readcost/hooks` (or `READCOST_HOOK_STATE`), owner-only, written by rename, ignored and deleted after a day. Read or write errors are logged and the hook carries on without memory.
- The Stop hook is unchanged: it already revises once per turn, and each turn is new text. git hooks and the generic protocol keep no memory.

Tests: `tests/test_hooks_repeat.py` uses made-up payloads for first report, silence on repeat, a reworded sentence keeping its finding, a new finding after a rewrite, block once, deny once followed by the PostToolUse note, Edit and Write sharing identities, a missing session id, `transcript_path`, session and subagent isolation, per-file isolation, `"always"`, five kinds of corrupted state, an unwritable state dir, stale state pruning, piku, and config validation. conftest points `READCOST_HOOK_STATE` at a temp dir so no test touches the real cache.

Not measured: the agent loop in docs/evaluation.md was not rerun with this change. Uncertain: PreToolUse uses per-finding memory, not per-set memory, so an attempt that only drops findings already denied is allowed rather than denied again. Two hooks running at once can lose each other's update, which only means a repeat report.

head: 468cbf6499e920c60e7263df3a6f71f23691ac14
source:
Experiment pull request. It adds an eval job and records the results; it changes no default behaviour.

Question: readcost's sentence constructions show no reader cost in any test so far. Do the patterns people complain about in model text (contrast framing, lists of three, restatement, uniform structure) track readers instead?

- `src/readcost/patterns.py`: detectors that read the parse and closed-class words, with no phrase lists. Nothing in readcost imports it; a test checks that.
- `scripts/eval_patterns.py` and the `patterns` job: rates for people and models writing to the same prompt (HAP-E, HC3), and tests against writers' edits and scores of model paragraphs (LAMP), users' preferences between two model answers (two Chatbot Arena sets) and reading times (EMTeC, OneStop, Provo). Construction findings go through the same tests with the same controls.

Results (docs/evaluation.md, "Discourse patterns and redundancy"):
- Instruction-tuned models write 2 to 4 times as many contrasts as the people they continue (GPT-4o 2.49 against 0.67 per 1,000 words). The base model does not.
- No counted pattern tracks any reader outcome once length and word frequency are held.
- Uniform sentence length, repeated openers and compressibility go with lower preference or more editing in three sets of model-only text, |rho| 0.06 to 0.12, with no multiple-comparison correction.
- Construction findings add at most 0.001 variance explained anywhere.

Recommendation: add none of the patterns, and keep the uniformity measures out until a test chosen in advance repeats them on technical text. The README's claim that findings mark sentences that cost readers time needs restating; that is a separate change.

Uncertain: no technical documentation in any reader set; about 20 measures against 9 outcomes, uncorrected.

head: 07ba689da763373f8ac336c636591467b5a5af2d
source:
Experiment; it changes no rule. It adds a `stack-terms` job to the eval workflow, two scripts, and the result in docs/evaluation.md ("Noun stacks: established term or coined?").

Why: stacked-nouns and hyphen-compound report established terms (`goroutine call stack`, `thread-state API`) as readily as coined stacks. The idea was to use word-pair counts to decide whether a stack is an attested term.

What was measured (job run of 18 Nov, one FineWeb-Edu shard, 799,175 documents):

- The shipped pair data cannot do this. `hyphen_pairs.txt.gz` holds hyphenated pairs only, without counts, so `scripts/build_open_pairs.py` counts open pairs ("call stack") instead.
- Labelled findings: 27 distinct stacked-nouns stacks (15 bench, 18 sample; 10 accepted, 37%, 95% interval 22 to 56) and 25 hyphen-compound (14 bench, 13 sample; 6 accepted, 24%, 11 to 43).
- Pair attestation does not separate accepted from rejected: AUC 0.58 and 0.53 for the weakest pair's PMI. "Every adjacent pair in 20+ documents with PMI 3+" drops 1 of 10 accepted and 4 of 17 rejected. Raters accepted stacks made of common pairs ("core team member").
- Bracketing by pair strength (adjacency or dependency model) predicts nothing.
- Recurrence in the document does not help; accepted stacks recur too.
- The whole stack as a phrase in 20+ documents drops 0 of 10 accepted and 3 of 17 rejected (precision 37% to 42%, intervals 22 to 56 and 24 to 61). That is the only candidate with no accepted loss, and three findings prove nothing.
- Web text holds none of the Go and CPython terms that cause the false positives.

So no exemption or setting is added. docs/research.md has the design for the human-label study: sample by evidence group, count in technical text too, ask raters whether the phrase is a known term, and the thresholds decided beforehand.

Uncertain: every label is a model rater's or one maintainer's; the sample join covers only findings the current rules still report; PMI uses a pair's document count as its frequency.

Also: `scripts/fetch_rulebench.py` now writes each source's sentences to `documents.jsonl`, which the recurrence test reads.

head: 4a62a7ddc4f64fb49d38f39ce4d37b5405a9538f
source:
Adds scripts that fetch a pinned evaluation corpus (13 essayists, language and framework docs, Hacker News and Stack Overflow answers, CPython and Rust std source, plus 42 READMEs and 1,000 Go commit messages) and score it offline. `docs/evaluation.md` reports the results.

Main result: of 210 sampled findings on this text, 3 are correct and 33 are correct or defensible. These labels come from one automated rater, with no second rater, and the texts were chosen for their clarity, so the result says where the rules break rather than how they do on model output. Causes, in order of volume:
- reduced object relatives with a pronoun subject ("someone I trust")
- settled and phrasal verbs counted as denominal ("figure out", "scale")
- comma counts read as inline lists
- verbs that normally take inanimate subjects ("the line feels")
- names in front of a noun counted as stacked nouns

The doc ranks 14 rule changes by how many findings each removes. They were simulated as filters, and none dropped a correct finding. They will land in follow-up PRs.

Fetched text goes under the ignored `ref/` directory; only derived statistics are in the repository.
